titre: “I Know That I Know Nothing”: What Socrates Really Says
accroche: The formula is not in the Apology. There Socrates says something else, narrower and less paradoxical, and he claims to know at least one point.
contenu_vulgarise:
Chaerephon, a friend of Socrates, went to Delphi to ask the Pythia whether there was a man wiser than Socrates. She answered that there was not. Socrates tells this to his judges, in Athens, at the trial where his life is at stake, and he confesses his bewilderment (21b, loose translation): “I am aware that I am wise neither a great deal nor a little.” Yet the god cannot lie. What does he mean?

## An Inquiry to Refute the Oracle

Socrates decides to refute the Pythia by finding a man wiser than himself. He goes to see a politician with a reputation for wisdom, questions him, and finds that he thinks himself wise without being so. As he walks away he says to himself (*Apology*, 21d, loose translation after Fowler): “I am wiser than this man; for neither of us knows anything fine and good, but he thinks he knows something when he does not, whereas I, as I do not know, do not think I know either.”

The advantage he grants himself is a small advantage, which he says himself he holds on this one small point. He does not boast of possessing a knowledge about his ignorance. He refuses to credit himself with a knowledge he does not have. Among the craftsmen, he even finds that they know many fine things, whereas he was aware of knowing nothing, so to speak (22c-d): on that point, they are wiser than he. Their flaw lies elsewhere: because they excel at their craft, they think themselves competent on the greatest questions. The sentence about the craftsmen is the closest to the famous formula, but it compares two competences; it does not state a thesis.

His conclusion comes later (23a-b). The god probably means that human wisdom is worth little, or even nothing, and he uses Socrates' name as an example: the wisest is the one who, like him, recognizes that he is worth nothing when it comes to wisdom. It speaks of the value of human knowledge, not of a knowledge about one's own nothingness.

## What He Says He Knows

Further on still (29b), Socrates declares that he does not know much about the other world and does not think he knows. Then he adds (loose translation): “But that to commit injustice and to disobey one better than oneself, god or man, is bad and shameful, that I know.” Someone who knew only that he knows nothing could not write that sentence.

## Where the Formula Comes From

In this Latin form, it is attested in Cicero, who writes more than three centuries after the trial. In the *Academica*, he has Varro speak, who sums up Socrates: he discussed without asserting anything himself, he said he knew nothing, except that very thing, and judged himself superior to others because they think they know what they do not, whereas he knows this alone, that he knows nothing (I, 16). It is a summary placed in a character's mouth, and the paradox is already there: to know that one knows nothing is to know something.

This summary dies hard. The introduction to Benjamin Jowett's English translation, which opens the *Apology* for modern readers, still writes that Socrates “knew nothing, and knew that he knew nothing.” Plato's text, for its part, describes a restraint: not claiming to know what one does not know. The formula makes it a thesis about knowledge, which Socrates did not state. What is lost when a restraint becomes a doctrine?

repere.texte: In the Academica (I, 16), Cicero has Varro say that Socrates “nihil se scire dicat nisi id ipsum”: he says he knows nothing, except that very thing. The dialogue was written more than three centuries after the death of Socrates (399 BCE).
repere.source: Cicero, Academica, ed. J. S. Reid, London, Macmillan, 1874, I, 15-16

carte.punch: “I know that I know nothing” is not a sentence from Plato's Apology.
carte.idee: In the Apology, Socrates says that, not knowing, he does not think he knows either (21d), and that he knows it is bad to commit injustice (29b). The Latin formula is attested in Cicero, more than three centuries after the trial.
carte.source_courte: Plato, Apology, 21d and 29b · Cicero, Academica, I, 16

quiz.question: What does Socrates say, at passage 21d of the Apology, about the politician he has just questioned?
choix: That he knows with certainty that he knows nothing, which the other does not know about himself
That neither of them can know anything, since all knowledge is impossible
That this man thinks he knows what he does not, whereas he himself does not think he knows
That the oracle was mistaken, since this politician is obviously wiser than he
quiz.explication: Socrates does not claim a knowledge about his ignorance: he notes that he does not credit himself with a knowledge he does not have, unlike the other. The first answer is Cicero's late summary, not Plato's text. The second attributes to Socrates a skepticism that he denies at 29b, where he says he knows that it is wrong to commit injustice. As for the oracle, the inquiry does not refute it: it confirms it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Socrates' account at his trial, what does the Pythia answer when Chaerephon asks her whether there is a man wiser than Socrates?
choix: That no man is wiser than he
That only the gods are wiser than men
That she cannot answer such a question
That the most renowned politician in Athens is
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Chaerephon goes to ask the oracle of Delphi whether there is a man wiser than Socrates, and the Pythia answers that there is not, which pushes Socrates to carry out his inquiry in order to refute her.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What flaw does Socrates find in the craftsmen he questions, at 22c-d of the Apology?
choix: They think themselves competent on everything, because of their excellence at their craft
They know many things about their craft, but refuse to admit it publicly
They know nothing about their own craft, despite their reputation in it
They judge themselves less wise than the politicians he had already questioned before them
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Socrates acknowledges that the craftsmen know fine things about their craft, but reproaches them for wrongly extending this competence to the greatest questions.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, where is the Latin formula first attested?
choix: In Cicero, in the Academica, centuries after Socrates
In Plato's Apology itself, at passage 21d
In a biography of Socrates written by his students
On an inscription found near the temple at Delphi
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry places the earliest attestation of the Latin formula in Cicero, in the Academica, where Varro sums it up, more than three centuries after the death of Socrates.
